In classical playing the two plates are held at 45 degrees with the dominant hand on top; before the stroke the arms open briefly and then the upper plate falls onto the lower one, the lower edges meeting first and the upper closing after, so that air does not get in the way. A beginner should first practise a steady grip and a consistent contact point, and then control the angle of the clash. Marching bands often use the Garfield grip, with the palms over the bells, which makes the cymbals easier to control and to flip; the hi-hat of a drum kit is worked with a pedal or with sticks.

Their development is tied closely to the needs of the ensemble: orchestral scores mark them a due to distinguish them from the suspended cymbal, and Russian composers developed a notation in which a plus sign and a circle denote the suspended cymbal and the clash cymbals respectively. In marching bands the “Garfield grip” is named after its use by the Garfield Cadets drum corps and makes visual moves such as flips and swings easier. The hi-hat of the drum kit came about because vaudeville theatre orchestras needed one player to cover bass drum, snare drum and cymbals, and that led to the modern drum kit. In recent years marching ensembles have tended to move the cymbals to the front ensemble, but indoor percussion ensembles still keep the clash cymbals.

The pitch changes with size and thickness: the smallest and thickest sound highest, thinner plates are more responsive, and the largest are the loudest. Holding them vertically with the inner faces towards the audience after the stroke shortens the ring; holding them parallel to the ground sends more sound out to the audience. Chinese-style clash cymbals have a rope through a square bell and can be released after the clash, which reduces damping and lengthens the ring, and the swinging produces a Doppler effect.
